Let $X$ be an LCH space with a fixed Radon measure $\mu$, and write
$C_c(X;\mathbb C)$ for the space of continuous complex-valued functions of
compact support ([[def-compact-support-c-c-and-c-zero-on-an-lch-space]]). A
complex-valued function on $X$ is **measurable** when its real and imaginary
parts are measurable, and it is **integrable** when its modulus is integrable
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). For
$p\in\{1,2\}$ the space $L^p(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ consists of the almost-everywhere
equivalence classes of measurable complex functions $f$ with
$$\|f\|_p:=\Bigl(\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu\Bigr)^{1/p}<\infty ,$$
the quotient and class notation being those of
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. The **modulus** $|f|$ of a
complex measurable function is measurable and depends only on the class of $f$
up to a null set, so $\|\cdot\|_p$ is well defined on classes; on classes it is
the norm of a complex normed space, and
$L^1(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ and $L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ are the complex Lebesgue
spaces used on this page.

Let now $G$ be an LCH group with a fixed left Haar measure $\mu$
([[def-left-haar-integral-and-left-haar-measure]]). Then
$C_c(G):=C_c(G;\mathbb C)$ and
$$L^p(G):=L^p(G,\mu;\mathbb C)\qquad(p\in\{1,2\}),$$
suppressing the measure from the notation; the Haar measure is kept fixed
throughout the page, so no ambiguity arises. The subscript is written
$\|f\|_1$ and $\|f\|_2$ for the two norms.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice for assertion 5 and the consequent
existence claim ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space
([[def-metric-space]]) and let $\mathcal{C}$ be the set of all Cauchy sequences
in $X$ ([[def-cauchy-in-metric]]). Then:

1. For all $x = (x_n)$ and $y = (y_n)$ in $\mathcal{C}$ the real sequence
   $\big(d(x_n,y_n)\big)_n$ converges, so
   $$\rho(x,y) \;:=\; \lim_{n} d(x_n,y_n)$$
   is a single well-determined real ([[thm-cauchy-criterion-via-lub]],
   [[lem-limit-unique]]).
2. The relation $x \sim y :\Longleftrightarrow \rho(x,y) = 0$ is an equivalence
   relation on $\mathcal{C}$. Write $\widehat{X} := \mathcal{C}/\!\sim$ for the
   set of its classes and $[x]$ for the class of $x$.
3. $\widehat{d}\big([x],[y]\big) := \rho(x,y)$ does not depend on the chosen
   representatives, and $\widehat{d}$ is a metric on $\widehat{X}$.
4. The map $\iota : X \to \widehat{X}$ sending $p$ to the class of the constant
   sequence at $p$ is an isometric embedding with dense image
   ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]],
   [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).
5. $(\widehat{X}, \widehat{d})$ is complete.

Consequently $\big((\widehat{X},\widehat{d}), \iota\big)$ is a completion of
$(X,d)$ ([[def-metric-completion]]), and **every metric space has a
completion**.

**The notation is kept honest.** A Cauchy sequence in $X$ need not converge in
$X$, so no symbol $\lim_n x_n$ appears anywhere below; the only limits taken are
limits of *real* sequences, and each is written only after its existence has been
proved. The equivalence relation is defined and verified here rather than cited, as was
done for [[def-integers]], so that the construction is self-contained and its
transitivity argument is visible at the point of use.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $X$ be a
normed space. The published metric completion of the norm metric on $X$ admits
a unique vector-space structure and norm whose induced metric is the
published completion metric and such that the constant sequence embedding
$i:X\to \widehat X$ is a dense linear isometry. With this structure,
$\widehat X$ is a Banach space.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ be a real or complex inner-product space and let $(\widehat X,\kappa)$ be its norm completion ([[def-completion-of-a-normed-space]]). Then $\widehat X$ carries a unique inner product that extends the given one along $\kappa$ and whose induced length is the completion norm; with it $\widehat X$ is a Hilbert space, and the extension is unique among inner products that extend the given pairing and induce the completion norm.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Write $\beta_n$ for the restriction of $\lambda_n$ to
the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Then $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is exactly the
completion domain of $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n), \beta_n)$
([[def-completion-of-a-measure-space]]), and $\lambda_n$ is the completed measure
there. Explicitly,

$$E \in \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) \iff E = A\cup N \text{ for some } A, Z \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \text{ with } N \subseteq Z \text{ and } \beta_n(Z) = 0,$$

and then $\lambda_n(E) = \beta_n(A)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $(X,\mathcal{A}_0,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$(X,\overline{\mathcal{A}_0},\overline{\mu})$ be its completion. If
$f : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ is measurable with respect to
$\overline{\mathcal{A}_0}$, then there is an $\mathcal{A}_0$-measurable function
$g : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ such that $f=g$ almost everywhere.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the product measure $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ and the Euclidean Lebesgue
measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ agree on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: Use finite Borel representatives as in [F2]. By [F3], the nonnegative function $|f(x)|^2\prod_{j=n+1}^m|\Omega(x_j)|^2$ is product-measurable, and Tonelli gives $\|J_{n,m}f\|_2^2=\|f\|_2^2\prod_{j=n+1}^m\|\Omega\|_2^2=\|f\|_2^2<\infty$. For $n=0$ the first factor is $|f|^2$, and $m=n$ is the identity map. Applying the same calculation to a difference shows independence of the representative of $f$; changing a representative of $\Omega$ changes the product only on finitely many null-coordinate cylinders, which are null by Tonelli and sigma-finiteness. Thus $J_{n,m}$ is a well-defined linear isometry on classes. Substitution gives $J_{m,r}J_{n,m}=J_{n,r}$. Computing two vectors' inner product at a common index is independent of a larger common index, since linear isometries preserve inner products by polarization. This defines a positive-definite inner product on the compatible union.

For $n\ge j$, write $x=(z,y)$ with $y=x_j$ and the other coordinates denoted by $z$. This coordinate permutation preserves Euclidean measure: on Borel rectangles both measures give the product of the side measures, so [F3] applies in this order too. Tonelli gives $\int\|f(z,\cdot)\|_2^2\,dz=\|f\|_2^2$, so almost every section lies in $L^2(\mathbb R)$. Set $a_f(z)=\int f(z,y)\overline{\Phi(y)}\,dy$ on those sections, and zero on the exceptional set. Cauchy--Schwarz gives $|a_f(z)|^2\le\|f(z,\cdot)\|_2^2$. Tonelli applied to the positive and negative parts of the real and imaginary integrand makes $a_f$ measurable; its section integral is finite almost everywhere by this estimate. Define $(P_{j,n}^\Phi f)(z,y)=a_f(z)\Phi(y)$. Tonelli now gives $\|P_{j,n}^\Phi f\|_2^2=\int|a_f|^2\le\|f\|_2^2$, and the same estimate for differences makes the map well-defined on classes. Since $\|\Phi\|_2=1$, section integration gives $a_{P_{j,n}^\Phi f}=a_f$, hence idempotence. The products $(P_{j,n}^\Phi f)\overline g$ and $f\overline{P_{j,n}^\Phi g}$ are integrable by Cauchy--Schwarz on $\mathbb R^n$; Fubini therefore yields $\langle P_{j,n}^\Phi f,g\rangle=\int a_f\overline{a_g}=\langle f,P_{j,n}^\Phi g\rangle$. Thus $P_{j,n}^\Phi$ is an orthogonal projection. When $n=j=1$, the $z$-space is the one-point space and the same formulas hold.

If $r\ge n\ge j$, the formula in step 1.2 acts on one of the first $n$ coordinates, while $J_{n,r}$ appends only factors $\Omega$ after coordinate $n$. Substitution in the integral formula gives $P_{j,r}^\Phi J_{n,r}=J_{n,r}P_{j,n}^\Phi$. For a vector initially represented in $H_n$ with $n<j$, first embed it in $H_j$; the compatibility identity shows that this and every later representation give the same image. Hence the projections define a contraction $P_j^\Phi$ on the compatible union. It extends uniquely by continuity to the Hilbert completion, and the identities of step 1.2 pass to limits, so the extension remains an orthogonal projection.
The compatible union is dense in its Hilbert completion by construction. Steps 1.1 and 2.1 prove, respectively, the well-defined incomplete tensor product and every stated local-projection property.

A **symplectic vector space** is a pair $(V,\omega)$ consisting of a
finite-dimensional real vector space $V$ and an alternating bilinear form
$\omega:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ for which

$$\omega^\flat:V\longrightarrow V^*,\qquad \omega^\flat(v)=\omega(v,\,·),$$

is an isomorphism. Equivalently, $\omega(v,w)=0$ for every $w\in V$ implies
$v=0$. The equivalence also follows from the radical clause in
[[thm-alternating-forms-have-a-symplectic-normal-form]]. The zero vector space,
with its unique alternating form, is included: its map to its dual is the
unique isomorphism.

Every symplectic vector space $(V,\omega)$ has dimension $2n$ for a unique
$n\ge 0$. It has a basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n,f_1,\ldots,f_n$ in which
$\omega(e_i,f_j)=\delta_{ij}$ and all $e$--$e$ and $f$--$f$ pairings vanish.

Every continuous group homomorphism $\varphi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb T$ from the
additive line to the multiplicative unit circle
([[lem-unit-circle-is-a-compact-metrizable-topological-group]]) is
$\varphi(t)=\exp(2\pi i\xi t)$ for a unique $\xi\in\mathbb R$; conversely every
such map $\varphi_{\xi}(t)=\exp(2\pi i\xi t)$ is a continuous character of the
additive line.

(1) For locally compact Hausdorff abelian groups $G_{1},\dots,G_{n}$ the map
$$\Phi:\widehat{G_{1}}\times\cdots\times\widehat{G_{n}}\to\widehat{G_{1}\times\cdots\times G_{n}},\qquad \Phi(\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{n})\big((x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\big):=\prod_{j}\gamma_{j}(x_{j}),$$
is an isomorphism of topological groups for the product topologies (choice-free,
finite $n$). (2) If $(G_{i})_{i\in I}$ is a family of discrete abelian groups and
$G=\bigoplus_{i}G_{i}$ is their algebraic direct sum equipped with the discrete
topology ([[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]), then, assuming the Axiom
of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), $\widehat G$ is topologically isomorphic to
the product $\prod_{i}\widehat{G_{i}}$ with the product topology. No claim is
made here about a direct sum carrying the subspace topology of the product of
non-discrete factors.

Let $N$ and $H$ be groups ([[def-group]]), and let $\alpha:H\to\operatorname{Aut}(N)$ be an action by automorphisms ([[def-action-by-automorphisms]]). The **external semidirect product** $N\rtimes_\alpha H$ is the set $N\times H$ with multiplication

$$(n,h)(n',h')=\bigl(n\alpha_h(n'),hh'\bigr).$$

When the action is clear, the subscript is omitted.

An **action of a group $H$ on a group $N$ by automorphisms** is a homomorphism

$$\alpha:H\longrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}(N).$$

Here automorphisms are those of [[def-group-isomorphism-and-automorphism]]. Writing $\alpha_h=\alpha(h)$, this means that every $\alpha_h$ is an automorphism of $N$, $\alpha_{hk}=\alpha_h\circ\alpha_k$, and $\alpha_1=\operatorname{id}_N$. Equivalently, by [[thm-group-actions-correspond-to-homomorphisms]], it is a group action ([[def-group-action]]) on the underlying set of $N$ for which every acting permutation is an automorphism.

Let $G$ be an abelian topological group ([[def-topological-group]]) written
additively, and let $\mathbb T=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ be the multiplicative
unit circle ([[lem-unit-circle-is-a-compact-metrizable-topological-group]]).

A **character** of $G$ is a continuous group homomorphism
$\gamma:G\to\mathbb T$ ([[def-group-homomorphism]],
[[def-continuous-map-top]]). The **Pontryagin dual** of $G$ is
$$\widehat G:=\operatorname{Hom}_{cts}(G,\mathbb T):=\{\gamma:G\to\mathbb T:\gamma\text{ is a continuous group homomorphism}\},$$
the set of characters, equipped with:

1. **Pointwise multiplication.** For $\gamma_1,\gamma_2\in\widehat G$ the
   product is $(\gamma_1\gamma_2)(x):=\gamma_1(x)\gamma_2(x)$ for every
   $x\in G$, with the constant character $x\mapsto1$ as its identity and
   $x\mapsto\gamma(x)^{-1}$ as the inverse of $\gamma$. With these operations
   the set of characters is a group, and it is abelian; this and the continuity
   of the two operations are proved in the next item, so no separate
   well-definedness obligation is left open here.
2. **Compact-open topology.** The topology is the compact-open topology
   inherited from $C(G,\mathbb T)$ ([[def-compact-open-topology-for-topological-domains]]),
   that is the subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]) for the
   subbasis
   $$S(K,V):=\{\gamma\in\widehat G:\gamma[K]\subseteq V\},\qquad K\subseteq G\text{ compact},\ V\subseteq\mathbb T\text{ open}.$$

The **evaluation pairing** is written
$$\langle x,\gamma\rangle:=\gamma(x)\in\mathbb T,\qquad x\in G,\ \gamma\in\widehat G .$$

The dual is written multiplicatively, so products of characters are written
$\gamma_1\gamma_2$ and the identity is written $1$. Through the topological
group isomorphism $\varepsilon:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\to\mathbb T$ of
[[lem-unit-circle-is-a-compact-metrizable-topological-group]], characters may
equivalently be viewed as continuous homomorphisms into the published circle
$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$; all statements below use the multiplicative circle
$\mathbb T$ and the compact-open subbasis displayed above.

derivations.claim: In coordinates from [F2], bilinearity gives $\omega((q,p),(q',p'))=q\cdot p'-p\cdot q'$. For three vectors $v,w,u$,$\omega(v,w)+\omega(v+w,u)=\omega(v,w)+\omega(v,u)+\omega(w,u) =\omega(w,u)+\omega(v,w+u).$Thus $c(v,w)=-\frac12\omega(v,w)$ satisfies the normalized 2-cocycle identity $c(v,w)+c(v+w,u)=c(w,u)+c(v,w+u)$. Substitution in the group law proves associativity; $\omega(v,0)=\omega(0,v)=0$ gives identity $(0,0)$, and $\omega(v,-v)=0$ gives inverse $(-v,-t)$. Addition and $\omega$ are continuous, so multiplication and inverse are continuous. The underlying finite-dimensional Euclidean space $V\times\mathbb R$ is locally compact and second countable.

An element $(v,t)$ commutes with every $(w,0)$ exactly when $\omega(v,w)=0$ for all $w$. Nondegeneracy in [F1] forces $v=0$, and each $(0,t)$ is central by the product formula. Hence the center is the displayed central coordinate. The projection $(v,t)\mapsto v$ is onto with kernel $\{(0,t):t\in\mathbb R\}$, proving exactness of the central extension in the definition.

For $q\in K$ and $(p,t)\in N$, direct multiplication gives $(q,0,0)(0,p,t)(-q,0,0)=(0,p,t-q\cdot p)$; thus $\alpha_q(p,t)=(p,t-q\cdot p)$. This is an automorphism because it is additive, has inverse $\alpha_{-q}$, and $\alpha_{q+q'}=\alpha_q\alpha_{q'}$. Every group element has the unique factorization$(q,p,z)=(0,p,z-q\cdot p/2)(q,0,0).$Therefore $(n,q)\mapsto n(q,0,0)$ is a bijection from the semidirect product of [F4] to $H(V,\omega)$; the conjugation computation makes it a homomorphism. Its coordinate formula and inverse are continuous, so it is a topological group isomorphism.

Apply [F3] to $N\cong\mathbb R^{n+1}$. Rescaling the coordinates by $2\pi$ gives every character exactly once as $\chi_{a,\mu}(p,t)=e^{i(a\cdot p+\mu t)}$. Since $\alpha_{-q}(p,t)=(p,t+q\cdot p)$, composition yields$q\cdot\chi_{a,\mu}=\chi_{a+\mu q,\mu}.$

The frequency parametrization in step 3.1 is a homeomorphism for the compact-open topology of [F5]. First consider $\beta_b(t)=e^{ibt}$ on $\mathbb R$. On any nonempty compact set $C\subset\mathbb R$, put $M=\max_{t\in C}|t|$; the estimate $|e^{ibt}-e^{ib_0t}|\le |b-b_0|M$ proves continuity uniformly on $C$. Conversely, for any $\delta>0$, require uniform distance less than $1$ from $\beta_{b_0}$ on the compact interval $[-\pi/\delta,\pi/\delta]$. If $|b-b_0|\ge\delta$, then $t=\pi/(b-b_0)$ lies in that interval and $|e^{i(b-b_0)t}-1|=2$, a contradiction. This compact-open neighborhood therefore forces $|b-b_0|<\delta$ and proves inverse continuity. Let $(V,\omega)$ be a finite-dimensional real symplectic vector space and let
$\lambda\in\mathbb R$. Regard the additive group underlying $V$ as discrete
for this construction, and define
$$m_\lambda(v,w):=e^{-i\lambda\omega(v,w)/2}.$$
Let $A_0(V,\omega,\lambda)=\mathbb C^{(V)}$ be the complex vector space of
finitely supported functions on $V$, with basis $(\delta_v)_{v\in V}$ and
unit $\delta_0$. Define
$$\delta_v\delta_w=m_\lambda(v,w)\delta_{v+w},\qquad \delta_v^*=\delta_{-v},$$
and extend multiplication bilinearly and the involution conjugate-linearly.
Here a linear functional $\varphi:A_0\to\mathbb C$ is **positive unital** if
$\varphi(a^*a)\ge0$ for every $a\in A_0$ and $\varphi(\delta_0)=1$. Put
$N_\varphi=\{a\in A_0:\varphi(a^*a)=0\}$, equip $A_0/N_\varphi$ with
$$\langle[a],[b]\rangle_\varphi:=\varphi(b^*a),$$
and let $\pi_\varphi$ be left multiplication on the Hilbert completion of
this quotient. The lemma
[[lem-universal-weyl-c-star-algebra-is-well-defined]] verifies that these
quotients and representations are well-defined.
Define the universal C*-seminorm and completion by
$$\|a\|_u:=\sup_{\varphi}\|\pi_\varphi(a)\|,\qquad C^*_{\mathrm W}(V,\omega,\lambda):=\overline{A_0/\ker\|\cdot\|_u}^{\,\|\cdot\|_u}.$$
The lemma [[lem-universal-weyl-c-star-algebra-is-well-defined]] proves that
the twisted algebra and GNS representations are well-defined, the seminorm is
finite and nonzero, and the completion is universal for unitary generators
with the displayed Weyl relations. Countable Choice is included through the
Hilbert completions in that construction.

A **possibly nonunital complex Banach algebra** is a complex vector space $A$
equipped with an associative complex-bilinear multiplication
$A \times A \to A$ ([[def-bounded-bilinear-map]] for the bilinearity convention)
and a norm under which $A$ is a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]],
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]), such that the norm is
**submultiplicative**:

$$\|ab\| \le \|a\|\,\|b\| \qquad (a,b \in A).$$

No multiplicative identity is assumed, and no real-algebra or unital
convention is imported from elsewhere.

A **complex C\*-algebra** is a possibly nonunital complex Banach algebra $A$
equipped with an **involution** $A \to A$, $a \mapsto a^*$, which is
conjugate-linear ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) and
satisfies

$$(a^*)^* = a, \qquad (ab)^* = b^*a^*, \qquad \|a^*a\| = \|a\|^2 \qquad (a,b \in A).$$

The last identity is the **C\*-identity**. Two immediate consequences are worth
recording, and both are proved from the displayed axioms alone:

- **the involution is isometric**: $\|a^*\| = \|a\|$. Indeed $\|a\|^2 = \|a^*a\| \le \|a^*\|\,\|a\|$ gives $\|a\| \le \|a^*\|$ when $a \ne 0$, and applying this inequality to $a^*$ and using $(a^*)^* = a$ gives $\|a^*\| \le \|a\|$; the case $a = 0$ is trivial;
- **no norm-uniqueness assertion is part of this definition**: such a theorem
  needs additional hypotheses and proof, and does not follow merely by naming
  the displayed C\*-identity.

Let $A$ and $B$ be complex C\*-algebras. A **bounded star-homomorphism**, or
bounded $*$-homomorphism, is a bounded complex-linear map
$\varphi : A \to B$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) satisfying

$$\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b), \qquad \varphi(a^*) = \varphi(a)^* \qquad (a,b \in A).$$

A star-homomorphism is **not** required to be unital, and it is not required
that a unit be present or preserved; when $A$ and $B$ both happen to be unital,
$\varphi$ is called **unital** if $\varphi(1_A) = 1_B$. The bounded nonunital
star-homomorphisms are the arrows of the locally compact duality theorem on this
page ([[thm-locally-compact-gelfand-duality]]), with properness imposed there
through [[def-approximate-unit-and-proper-c-star-morphism]].

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A $\mathbb K$-linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice for assertion 5 and the consequent
existence claim ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space
([[def-metric-space]]) and let $\mathcal{C}$ be the set of all Cauchy sequences
in $X$ ([[def-cauchy-in-metric]]). Then:

1. For all $x = (x_n)$ and $y = (y_n)$ in $\mathcal{C}$ the real sequence
   $\big(d(x_n,y_n)\big)_n$ converges, so
   $$\rho(x,y) \;:=\; \lim_{n} d(x_n,y_n)$$
   is a single well-determined real ([[thm-cauchy-criterion-via-lub]],
   [[lem-limit-unique]]).
2. The relation $x \sim y :\Longleftrightarrow \rho(x,y) = 0$ is an equivalence
   relation on $\mathcal{C}$. Write $\widehat{X} := \mathcal{C}/\!\sim$ for the
   set of its classes and $[x]$ for the class of $x$.
3. $\widehat{d}\big([x],[y]\big) := \rho(x,y)$ does not depend on the chosen
   representatives, and $\widehat{d}$ is a metric on $\widehat{X}$.
4. The map $\iota : X \to \widehat{X}$ sending $p$ to the class of the constant
   sequence at $p$ is an isometric embedding with dense image
   ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]],
   [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).
5. $(\widehat{X}, \widehat{d})$ is complete.

Consequently $\big((\widehat{X},\widehat{d}), \iota\big)$ is a completion of
$(X,d)$ ([[def-metric-completion]]), and **every metric space has a
completion**.

**The notation is kept honest.** A Cauchy sequence in $X$ need not converge in
$X$, so no symbol $\lim_n x_n$ appears anywhere below; the only limits taken are
limits of *real* sequences, and each is written only after its existence has been
proved. The equivalence relation is defined and verified here rather than cited, as was
done for [[def-integers]], so that the construction is self-contained and its
transitivity argument is visible at the point of use.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $X$ be a
normed space. The published metric completion of the norm metric on $X$ admits
a unique vector-space structure and norm whose induced metric is the
published completion metric and such that the constant sequence embedding
$i:X\to \widehat X$ is a dense linear isometry. With this structure,
$\widehat X$ is a Banach space.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ be a real or complex inner-product space and let $(\widehat X,\kappa)$ be its norm completion ([[def-completion-of-a-normed-space]]). Then $\widehat X$ carries a unique inner product that extends the given one along $\kappa$ and whose induced length is the completion norm; with it $\widehat X$ is a Hilbert space, and the extension is unique among inner products that extend the given pairing and induce the completion norm.

Assume Countable Choice. For every nonzero complex Hilbert space $H$, $\mathcal B(H)$, with the operator norm, composition, identity, and Hilbert adjoint, is a unital C\*-algebra and $\|T^*T\|=\|T\|^2$.

derivations.claim: Bilinearity gives $m_\lambda(v,w)m_\lambda(v+w,z)=m_\lambda(w,z)m_\lambda(v,w+z)$, so the two parenthesizations of $\delta_v\delta_w\delta_z$ agree. Also $m_\lambda(0,v)=m_\lambda(v,0)=1$, so $\delta_0$ is a two-sided unit. Since $\omega(v,-v)=0$, $\delta_v^*\delta_v=\delta_v\delta_v^*=\delta_0$. Finally, $\overline{m_\lambda(v,w)}=m_\lambda(-w,-v)$, which gives $(\delta_v\delta_w)^*=\delta_w^*\delta_v^*$; by bilinearity and conjugate-linearity these identities extend to all finite sums.

For any positive unital $\varphi$, the form $B_\varphi(a,b)=\varphi(b^*a)$ is positive semidefinite. Positivity of $B_\varphi(a+tb,a+tb)$ for every complex $t$ gives $|B_\varphi(a,b)|^2\le B_\varphi(a,a)B_\varphi(b,b)$: if $B_\varphi(b,b)>0$, minimize the quadratic in $t$; if it is zero, varying the phase and magnitude of $t$ forces $B_\varphi(a,b)=0$. Therefore its null space $N_\varphi=\{a:B_\varphi(a,a)=0\}$ is orthogonal to every vector and the quotient has the inner product specified in [F1].

Write $a=\sum_v a_v\delta_v$ with finite support and define $\varphi_0(a)=a_0$. The coefficient of $\delta_0$ in $a^*a$ is $\sum_v\overline{a_v}a_vm_\lambda(-v,v)=\sum_v|a_v|^2$, because $\omega(v,-v)=0$. Thus $\varphi_0(a^*a)\ge0$ and $\varphi_0(\delta_0)=1$; the positive unital functional set in [F1] is nonempty.

Left multiplication by $\delta_v$ is an isometry on this quotient: $B_\varphi(\delta_va,\delta_va)=\varphi(a^*\delta_v^*\delta_va)=\varphi(a^*a)=B_\varphi(a,a)$. Hence it preserves the null space. For a finite sum $a=\sum_v a_v\delta_v$, the triangle inequality gives $\|L_a[b]\|\le(\sum_v|a_v|)\|[b]\|$. Left multiplication therefore extends to a bounded operator on the Hilbert completion of the quotient, and its adjoint is $L_{a^*}$ because $B_\varphi(ab,c)=B_\varphi(b,a^*c)$. Associativity from step 1.1 makes $\pi_\varphi(a):=L_a$ a unital $*$-representation.

The supremum in [F1] is over a set of functionals (a subset of the function set $\mathbb C^{A_0}$), is nonempty by step 2.1, and is finite since step 2.2 gives $\|\pi_\varphi(a)\|\le\sum_v|a_v|$ for every $\varphi$. Each GNS Hilbert space is nonzero because $\|[\delta_0]\|^2=\varphi(\delta_0)=1$, so [F3] applies to every $\pi_\varphi$. Since each $\pi_\varphi$ is a $*$-representation, $\|a^*a\|_u=\sup_\varphi\|\pi_\varphi(a)^*\pi_\varphi(a)\|=\sup_\varphi\|\pi_\varphi(a)\|^2=\|a\|_u^2$. Submultiplicativity and $\|a^*\|_u=\|a\|_u$ follow by the same operator-norm calculation. Thus $\|\cdot\|_u$ is a nonzero C*-seminorm; its kernel is a $*$-ideal, and the induced norm on $A_0/\ker\|\cdot\|_u$ is a C*-norm.

Let $\rho:A_0\to\mathcal B(\mathcal K)$ be any unital $*$-representation. If $\mathcal K=\{0\}$, the unique zero representation extends; assume otherwise and choose a unit vector $\xi\in\mathcal K$. The vector functional $\varphi_\xi(a)=\langle\rho(a)\xi,\xi\rangle$ is positive and unital. The map $[a]\mapsto\rho(a)\xi$ preserves the inner product on the GNS quotient, extends to a unitary from its completion onto the cyclic subspace $\overline{\rho(A_0)\xi}$, and intertwines $\pi_{\varphi_\xi}$ with the restriction of $\rho$. Therefore $\|\rho(a)\xi\|\le\|\pi_{\varphi_\xi}(a)\|\le\|a\|_u$; taking the supremum over unit vectors gives $\|\rho(a)\|\le\|a\|_u$.

The quotient completion in [F1] is a C*-algebra: multiplication and $*$ extend continuously by submultiplicativity and isometry, and the C*-identity passes to limits. Step 4.1 makes every unital $*$-representation contractive for $\|\cdot\|_u$, so it extends uniquely to the completion; conversely each representation of the completion restricts to one of $A_0$. The state $\varphi_0$ from step 2.1 sends $\delta_0$ to a unit vector in its GNS space, so $\|\delta_0\|_u=1$ and the completion is nonzero. This proves the universal property and all claims.

Let $(V,\omega)$ be a finite-dimensional real symplectic vector space, so $V$
is a finite-dimensional real vector space and $\omega:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ is
an alternating, nondegenerate bilinear form
([[def-symplectic-vector-space]]). Define
$$H(V,\omega):=V\times\mathbb R$$with the product topology and multiplication$$
(v,t)(w,s)=\left(v+w,\ t+s-\frac12\omega(v,w)\right).
$$
The proposed identity is $(0,0)$, and the central coordinate is the subgroup
$j(\mathbb R)=\{(0,t):t\in\mathbb R\}$. The lemma
[[lem-heisenberg-group-lagrangian-splitting-and-dual-orbit]] verifies that this
is a second-countable locally compact topological group and that $j(\mathbb R)$
is its center.

The maps $j(t)=(0,t)$ and $\operatorname{pr}_V(v,t)=v$ form the central
extension shown below. The diagram records the maps; exactness is established
by the explicit kernel computation in the cited lemma.

```tikzcd
1 \arrow[r] & \mathbb R \arrow[r, hook, "j"] & H(V,\omega) \arrow[r, two heads, "\operatorname{pr}_V"] & V \arrow[r] & 1
```

Fix a finite-dimensional real symplectic vector space $(V,\omega)$ and a real
parameter $\lambda$. A **Weyl system with parameter $\lambda$** on a nonzero
complex Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ is a map $W:V\to U(\mathcal H)$ such that
$$W(0)=I,\qquad W(v)W(w)=e^{-i\lambda\omega(v,w)/2}W(v+w)\quad(v,w\in V).$$
It is **regular** when, for every $v\in V$, the map
$t\mapsto W(tv)$ is strongly continuous on $\mathbb R$. It is
**irreducible** when the only closed subspaces invariant under every $W(v)$ are
$\{0\}$ and $\mathcal H$, as in
[[def-strongly-continuous-unitary-representation]].

Each $W(v)$ is unitary. Substituting $w=-v$ in the relation gives
$W(v)W(-v)=I$, because $\omega(v,-v)=0$; hence
$W(v)^*=W(-v)$. The scalar $\lambda$ is the central character parameter:
the associated representation of [[def-heisenberg-group-of-a-symplectic-vector-space]]
acts on $(0,t)$ by $e^{i\lambda t}I$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Then

$$\|\tau_h f-f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(h \to 0).$$

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume countable choice. If $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ and $\widehat f\in L^1$, then
$$g(x)=\int\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi$$
is bounded and continuous, equals f almost everywhere, and equals the specified value at every Lebesgue point of f.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Write $\beta_n$ for the restriction of $\lambda_n$ to
the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Then $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is exactly the
completion domain of $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n), \beta_n)$
([[def-completion-of-a-measure-space]]), and $\lambda_n$ is the completed measure
there. Explicitly,

$$E \in \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) \iff E = A\cup N \text{ for some } A, Z \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \text{ with } N \subseteq Z \text{ and } \beta_n(Z) = 0,$$

and then $\lambda_n(E) = \beta_n(A)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $(X,\mathcal{A}_0,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$(X,\overline{\mathcal{A}_0},\overline{\mu})$ be its completion. If
$f : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ is measurable with respect to
$\overline{\mathcal{A}_0}$, then there is an $\mathcal{A}_0$-measurable function
$g : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ such that $f=g$ almost everywhere.

Let $\tilde f,\tilde g : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be Borel measurable
functions. Then

$$ H(x,y) := \tilde f(x-y)\tilde g(y) $$

is Borel measurable on $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$. In particular, for each fixed
$x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, the section $y \mapsto H(x,y)$ is measurable.

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), let $c$ be a nonzero real and write
$cE := \{\, cx : x \in E \,\}$ for $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, where
$(cx)_i := cx_i$. Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(cE) = |c|^{\,n}\,\lambda_n^*(E)$ for every subset $E$, the
   product being defined in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|c|^{\,n} > 0$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $cE$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(cE) = |c|^{\,n}\lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

At $c = -1$ the map is reflection in the origin and $|c|^{\,n} = 1$, so it
preserves outer measure, measurability and measure. The value $c = 0$ is
excluded because $0E$ is $\{0\}$ or $\varnothing$ and carries no information
about $E$.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

$$\big(S_\lambda(q,p,t)f\big)(x) =e^{i\lambda t+i\lambda p\cdot(x-q/2)}f(x-q).$$
Then $S_\lambda$ is a strongly continuous unitary representation of [[def-heisenberg-group-of-a-symplectic-vector-space]], has central character $t\mapsto e^{i\lambda t}$, and its Weyl operators form an irreducible regular Weyl system with phase $e^{-i\lambda\omega/2}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on
$(X,\Sigma)$, and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be bounded and $\Sigma$-measurable
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). Then:

1. there is a unique operator $\Phi_E(f)\in\mathcal B(H)$ with
   $$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,y\rangle=\int f\,dE_{x,y}\qquad(x,y\in H),$$
   and for every sequence $(s_n)$ of complex simple functions with
   $\|f-s_n\|_\infty\to0$ one has $\|\Phi_E(f)-\int s_n\,dE\|\to0$: the integral
   is obtained from uniform simple approximations and is independent of the
   approximating sequence;
2. $\|\Phi_E(f)\|\le\|f\|_\infty$, and for every $x\in H$
$$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,x\rangle=\int f\,dE_x,\qquad \|\Phi_E(f)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,dE_x ;$$
3. the exact norm is the **$E$-essential supremum**
$$\|f\|_{E,\infty}:=\sup\bigl\{\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}:\ x\in H,\ \|x\|=1\bigr\}, \qquad \|\Phi_E(f)\|=\|f\|_{E,\infty},$$
   where $\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}$ denotes the essential supremum of the real measurable function $|f|$ with respect to
   the finite measure $E_x$ ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]).

Assume AC. Every second-countable locally compact Hausdorff space is Polish,
hence standard Borel. Consequently, if $G$ is a second-countable locally
compact Hausdorff topological group and $H\le G$ is a closed subgroup, then
the homogeneous space $G/H$ with its quotient topology is Polish and the
quotient Borel structure together with the left action
$G\times G/H\to G/H$ is a standard Borel $G$-space with Borel action.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space
([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]) and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A **projection valued measure** (PVM) on
$(X,\Sigma)$ is a map

$$E:\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal B(H),\qquad B\longmapsto E(B),$$

such that:

1. $E(B)$ is an **orthogonal projection** for every $B\in\Sigma$, that is, a
   bounded operator with $E(B)^2=E(B)=E(B)^*$; there is no finite-dimensional
   restriction;
2. $E(\varnothing)=0$ and $E(X)=I$;
3. $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ for all $B,C\in\Sigma$;
4. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$ with
   union $B$ and every $x\in H$, the series $\sum_nE(B_n)x$ converges in norm
   to $E(B)x$, that is
   $$E(B)x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E(B_n)x .$$

Clause 4 is **strong countable additivity**. A PVM is called **regular** when
$X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), the
$\sigma$-algebra is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and every one of the finite
positive measures

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad x\in H,\ B\in\Sigma,$$

is a regular Borel measure ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]). Inner
products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); this fixed convention is the one
used for every pairing $E_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ on this page.

**Well-definedness: the projection clause.** The conditions $P^2=P=P^*$ are
simultaneously meaningful and describe exactly the Hilbert orthogonal
projections, with no hidden finite-dimensional hypothesis. Indeed, for a
bounded $P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ the range $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a linear
subspace, and for $y=Pw$ one has
$\langle x-Px,y\rangle=\langle P(x-Px),w\rangle=\langle Px-P^2x,w\rangle=0$, so
$x-Px\perp\operatorname{ran}P$; conversely $\langle Pz,Pz\rangle=\langle z,P^*Pz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle=0$
for $z\perp\operatorname{ran}P$, so $z\in\ker P$, while
$\langle z,Px\rangle=\langle Pz,x\rangle=0$ for $z\in\ker P$ gives
$\ker P=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$
([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Hence
$\operatorname{ran}P=(\ker P)^\perp$ is closed, and the two defining properties
$Px\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $x-Px\in(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ of
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]] show that $P=P_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is
the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace, and conversely every
such $P_M$ is idempotent and self-adjoint by
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]] and
[[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]. Finally $P$ is
contractive: from $\langle Px,x\rangle=\langle Px,Px\rangle=\|Px\|^2$ and
Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Px\|^2\le\|Px\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$,
and $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$ is a nonnegative real number.

**Well-definedness: the regularity clause.** For an orthogonal projection value
the pairing $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real number and
$E_x(X)=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2<+\infty$, so every $E_x$ is a finite
nonnegative set function and the regularity requirement is a meaningful
condition on it; that each $E_x$ is genuinely a countably additive measure of
total mass $\|x\|^2$, and that the polarized pairings $E_{x,y}$ are finite
complex measures, is proved as
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]] before either is used.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume AC. For $g\in G$ and $F\in C_c(G,H;V)$, define $(\Pi_\rho(g)F)(x)=D_g(xH)^{1/2}F(g^{-1}x)=[\rho(g^{-1}x)/\rho(x)]^{1/2}F(g^{-1}x)$. This is covariant, preserves the inner product, satisfies $\Pi_\rho(g_1)\Pi_\rho(g_2)=\Pi_\rho(g_1g_2)$, and extends to a unitary on the completion.

derivations.claim: Fix a symplectic basis from [F1], identify $V$ with $\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n$, and define$\pi(v,t):=e^{i\lambda t}W(v)\quad((v,t)\in H(V,\omega)).$The Weyl relation and the group product in [F2] give$\pi(v,t)\pi(w,s)=e^{i\lambda(t+s)-i\lambda\omega(v,w)/2}W(v+w)=\pi(v+w,t+s-\omega(v,w)/2),$so $\pi$ is a unitary group representation with central character $\pi(0,t)=e^{i\lambda t}I$. It is strongly continuous: if $v=\sum_{j=1}^n(q_je_j+p_jf_j)$, repeatedly apply the Weyl relation in this fixed coordinate order to express $W(v)$ as a finite product of $W(q_je_j)$ and $W(p_jf_j)$ times a scalar phase. That phase is an exponential of a finite sum of bilinear coordinate terms, hence is continuous; each line factor is strongly continuous by regularity. Finite products of strongly continuous unitaries are strongly continuous by inserting and subtracting one factor at a time. Its invariant closed subspaces are exactly those of $W$, since the central factor is scalar, so $\pi$ is irreducible.

The representation space is separable. Choose $\xi\ne0$. The closed span of $\pi(G)\xi$ is a nonzero invariant subspace, hence equals $\mathcal H$ by irreducibility. The group $G=H(V,\omega)$ is homeomorphic to $\mathbb R^{2n+1}$, so the rational-coordinate points give a countable dense subset $D$. Strong continuity makes $\{\pi(g)\xi:g\in D\}$ dense in the orbit of $\xi$; its finite rational-complex linear span is countable and dense in $\mathcal H$. Therefore [F3] applies.

Write $G=N\rtimes K$ as in [F2], and let $\tau(q)=\pi(q,0,0)$ denote the representation of $K$. Conjugation in the semidirect product gives $\tau(q)\pi(n)\tau(q)^{-1}=\pi(\alpha_q(n))$ for every $n\in N$. By [F3] there is a unique regular PVM $P$ on $\widehat N$ with$\pi(n)=\int_{\widehat N}\chi(n)\,dP(\chi),\qquad \tau(q)P(E)\tau(q)^{-1}=P(q\cdot E).$

The central subgroup is $z_t=(0,0,t)$, and $\pi(z_t)=e^{i\lambda t}I$. For each rational $t$, let $E_t=\{\chi\in\widehat N:\chi(z_t)=e^{i\lambda t}\}$, a Borel set. The SNAG formula in [F3] gives $\Phi_P(\chi\mapsto\chi(z_t)-e^{i\lambda t})=0$. By the norm-square identity in [F9], each scalar measure $P_\xi$ assigns integral zero to $|\chi(z_t)-e^{i\lambda t}|^2$, so it is supported on $E_t$ and $P(E_t)=I$. Since $\mathbb Q$ is countable and $P$ is countably additive, $P(\bigcap_{t\in\mathbb Q}E_t)=I$. Every character of $N\cong\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is continuous in its real parameter, so equality on rational $t$ implies that this intersection is precisely $\widehat N_\lambda$ from [F2]. Hence $P(\widehat N_\lambda)=I$.

The orbit map $q\mapsto q\cdot\chi_{0,\lambda}=\chi_{\lambda q,\lambda}$ is a bijection by [F2]. It is a homeomorphism for the compact-open topology: $|e^{iu}-e^{iv}|\le|u-v|$ gives uniform convergence on each compact subset of $N$ when the frequency parameters converge. Conversely, for $\delta>0$ and any frequency coordinate, uniform distance less than $1$ from a fixed character on the compact coordinate segment $|t|\le\pi/\delta$ forces the corresponding frequency difference $b$ to satisfy $|b|<\delta$: otherwise $t=\pi/b$ lies in that segment and the distance is $2$. The finite-product dual identification in [F2] therefore has continuous inverse, and scaling by $\lambda\ne0$ identifies $G/N\cong K$ homeomorphically with $\widehat N_\lambda$. Since $G/N\cong K\cong\mathbb R^n$, [F10] gives its standard Borel structure and Borel $G$-action. Push $P$ through this Borel isomorphism to obtain a PVM on $G/N$. Its covariance is the second identity in step 2.2, and its total projection is $I$ by step 3.1. Thus $(\pi,P)$ is a transitive system of imprimitivity on $G/N$ in the sense of [F4]. Mackey's theorem yields a strongly continuous unitary representation $\sigma:N\to U(K_0)$ on a separable Hilbert space and a unitary intertwiner from $\pi$ to $\operatorname{Ind}_N^G\sigma$.

Let $s(q)=(q,0,0)$ be the section of $G/N$. The normalized measure $\mu$ in the induced model is Radon and finite on compact sets by [F4]. Under $G/N\cong\mathbb R^n$, the compact boxes $[-m,m]^n$ (or the singleton when $n=0$) form a countable cover, so $\mu$ is $\sigma$-finite. The base is standard Borel by [F10], and the constant fiber $K_0$ is separable, so the hypotheses of [F7] hold. For each $n\in N$, Mackey's PVM identification in [F4] sends $P(E)$ to multiplication by $\mathbf1_E$; the bounded Borel integral result [F9] therefore sends the SNAG integral of $\chi\mapsto\chi(n)$ to multiplication by $q\mapsto\chi_{\lambda q,\lambda}(n)$. In the induced model the action of $n$ on the fiber at $q$ is $\sigma(s(q)^{-1}ns(q))=\sigma(\alpha_{-q}(n))$ by [F5]. Equality of the two multiplication operators and [F7] give$\sigma(\alpha_{-q}(n))=\chi_{\lambda q,\lambda}(n)I_{K_0}\quad\text{for almost every }q$. In the coordinates $N=\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R$, set $D_N=\mathbb Q^n\times\mathbb Q$, a countable dense subset. Intersecting the corresponding conull sets gives one conull set $E\subset K$ on which the equality holds for every $n\in D_N$. The normalized measure class on $G/N$ has full support by [F4], so $E$ is dense. For fixed $n\in D_N$, both sides are continuous in $q$; equality on $E$ extends to $q=0$, giving $\sigma(n)=\chi_{0,\lambda}(n)I_{K_0}$. Strong continuity of $\sigma$ and continuity of $\chi_{0,\lambda}$ extend this equality from $D_N$ to all $N$.

If $K_0$ had a nonzero proper closed subspace $L$, then [F11] gives $K_0=L\oplus L^\perp$ with $L^\perp\ne0$. Both subspaces are invariant under the scalar action $\sigma(n)=\chi_{0,\lambda}(n)I$. In the induced model the sections valued in $L$ form a closed invariant subspace: the pointwise orthogonal projection onto $L$ is bounded, and the scalar fiber action preserves it. By [F4], choose a nonempty relatively compact open subset $U\subseteq G/N$; full support and Radon finiteness give $0<\mu(U)<\infty$. For nonzero $\ell\in L$ and $r\in L^\perp$, the sections $\mathbf1_U\ell$ and $\mathbf1_Ur$ are nonzero elements of the two respective subspaces. This contradicts irreducibility of $\pi$. Thus $K_0$ is one-dimensional and $\sigma$ is equivalent to $\chi_{0,\lambda}$. The Schrödinger model in [F8] is strongly continuous and irreducible on the second-countable group $G$; choosing a nonzero vector and using a countable dense subset of $G$ as in step 2.1 shows that $L^2(\mathbb R^n)$ is separable. Its position projections $P_0(E):=M_{\mathbf1_E}$ form a PVM by [F12], and covariance follows because translations shift these projections while modulation operators commute with them. Translations act transitively on $G/N$, so $(\pi_0,P_0)$ is a transitive system on the standard Borel quotient from [F10]. Mackey's theorem [F4] induces it from some strongly continuous $\sigma_0:N\to U(K_1)$. For $n=(0,p,t)\in N$, the explicit Schrödinger formula acts by multiplication by $\chi_{\lambda x,\lambda}(n)$. In the induced model, [F5] gives the fiber field $\sigma_0(\alpha_{-x}(n))$. Since the intertwiner also identifies $P_0$ with multiplication by indicators, [F7] shows these fields agree almost everywhere. The dense-set and continuity argument of step 5.1 gives $\sigma_0(n)=\chi_{0,\lambda}(n)I_{K_1}$ for all $n\in N$. The nonzero Schrödinger space forces $K_1\ne0$; the same invariant-subspace argument used above for $K_0$, now using irreducibility from [F8], forces $\dim K_1=1$. Thus $\sigma_0$ is equivalent to the one-dimensional character $\chi_{0,\lambda}$.

The uniqueness clause [F6] now identifies the transitive systems of $\pi$ and the Schrödinger model, because their inducing representations are both equivalent to $\chi_{0,\lambda}$. Hence the underlying unitary representations are unitarily equivalent; restricting the intertwiner to $(v,0)$ gives unitary equivalence of the Weyl systems. Existence and irreducibility of the model are [F8], so this proves the unique equivalence class for the fixed $\lambda\ne0$. The argument does not apply to zero central parameter or to infinite-dimensional phase space.

Let $(V,\omega)$ be a finite-dimensional real symplectic vector space and let
$\lambda\in\mathbb R$. Regard the additive group underlying $V$ as discrete
for this construction, and define
$$m_\lambda(v,w):=e^{-i\lambda\omega(v,w)/2}.$$
Let $A_0(V,\omega,\lambda)=\mathbb C^{(V)}$ be the complex vector space of
finitely supported functions on $V$, with basis $(\delta_v)_{v\in V}$ and
unit $\delta_0$. Define
$$\delta_v\delta_w=m_\lambda(v,w)\delta_{v+w},\qquad \delta_v^*=\delta_{-v},$$
and extend multiplication bilinearly and the involution conjugate-linearly.
Here a linear functional $\varphi:A_0\to\mathbb C$ is **positive unital** if
$\varphi(a^*a)\ge0$ for every $a\in A_0$ and $\varphi(\delta_0)=1$. Put
$N_\varphi=\{a\in A_0:\varphi(a^*a)=0\}$, equip $A_0/N_\varphi$ with
$$\langle[a],[b]\rangle_\varphi:=\varphi(b^*a),$$
and let $\pi_\varphi$ be left multiplication on the Hilbert completion of
this quotient. The lemma
[[lem-universal-weyl-c-star-algebra-is-well-defined]] verifies that these
quotients and representations are well-defined.
Define the universal C*-seminorm and completion by
$$\|a\|_u:=\sup_{\varphi}\|\pi_\varphi(a)\|,\qquad C^*_{\mathrm W}(V,\omega,\lambda):=\overline{A_0/\ker\|\cdot\|_u}^{\,\|\cdot\|_u}.$$
The lemma [[lem-universal-weyl-c-star-algebra-is-well-defined]] proves that
the twisted algebra and GNS representations are well-defined, the seminorm is
finite and nonzero, and the completion is universal for unitary generators
with the displayed Weyl relations. Countable Choice is included through the
Hilbert completions in that construction.

Let $A_0(V,\omega,\lambda)$, its positive unital functional set, and
$\|\cdot\|_u$ be as in
[[def-universal-weyl-c-star-algebra]]. Under Countable Choice, the twisted
multiplication and involution make $A_0$ a unital $*$-algebra, the displayed
supremum is a finite nonzero C*-seminorm, and its kernel quotient completion is
the universal C*-algebra generated by unitaries $u_v$ with
$$u_vu_w=e^{-i\lambda\omega(v,w)/2}u_{v+w},\qquad u_v^*=u_{-v}.$$
Every unital $*$-representation of the algebraic relations extends uniquely to
a bounded $*$-representation of this completion. No strong continuity of
$v\mapsto u_v$ is part of this universal property.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice for assertion 5 and the consequent
existence claim ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space
([[def-metric-space]]) and let $\mathcal{C}$ be the set of all Cauchy sequences
in $X$ ([[def-cauchy-in-metric]]). Then:

1. For all $x = (x_n)$ and $y = (y_n)$ in $\mathcal{C}$ the real sequence
   $\big(d(x_n,y_n)\big)_n$ converges, so
   $$\rho(x,y) \;:=\; \lim_{n} d(x_n,y_n)$$
   is a single well-determined real ([[thm-cauchy-criterion-via-lub]],
   [[lem-limit-unique]]).
2. The relation $x \sim y :\Longleftrightarrow \rho(x,y) = 0$ is an equivalence
   relation on $\mathcal{C}$. Write $\widehat{X} := \mathcal{C}/\!\sim$ for the
   set of its classes and $[x]$ for the class of $x$.
3. $\widehat{d}\big([x],[y]\big) := \rho(x,y)$ does not depend on the chosen
   representatives, and $\widehat{d}$ is a metric on $\widehat{X}$.
4. The map $\iota : X \to \widehat{X}$ sending $p$ to the class of the constant
   sequence at $p$ is an isometric embedding with dense image
   ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]],
   [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).
5. $(\widehat{X}, \widehat{d})$ is complete.

Consequently $\big((\widehat{X},\widehat{d}), \iota\big)$ is a completion of
$(X,d)$ ([[def-metric-completion]]), and **every metric space has a
completion**.

**The notation is kept honest.** A Cauchy sequence in $X$ need not converge in
$X$, so no symbol $\lim_n x_n$ appears anywhere below; the only limits taken are
limits of *real* sequences, and each is written only after its existence has been
proved. The equivalence relation is defined and verified here rather than cited, as was
done for [[def-integers]], so that the construction is self-contained and its
transitivity argument is visible at the point of use.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $X$ be a
normed space. The published metric completion of the norm metric on $X$ admits
a unique vector-space structure and norm whose induced metric is the
published completion metric and such that the constant sequence embedding
$i:X\to \widehat X$ is a dense linear isometry. With this structure,
$\widehat X$ is a Banach space.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ be a real or complex inner-product space and let $(\widehat X,\kappa)$ be its norm completion ([[def-completion-of-a-normed-space]]). Then $\widehat X$ carries a unique inner product that extends the given one along $\kappa$ and whose induced length is the completion norm; with it $\widehat X$ is a Hilbert space, and the extension is unique among inner products that extend the given pairing and induce the completion norm.

derivations.claim: On basis vectors of the finite-support subspace of $\ell^2(V)$ define $L_v\delta_x=m_\lambda(v,x)\delta_{v+x}$. Since $|m_\lambda(v,x)|=1$ and $x\mapsto v+x$ is a bijection of $V$, $L_v$ preserves the inner product and maps finite-support vectors to finite-support vectors. It extends to $\ell^2(V)$ by $L_v[(a_n)]=[(L_va_n)]$ on Cauchy-sequence classes; the extension is unitary with inverse $L_{-v}$. The cocycle identity gives $L_vL_w\delta_x=m_\lambda(w,x)m_\lambda(v,w+x)\delta_{v+w+x}=m_\lambda(v,w)m_\lambda(v+w,x)\delta_{v+w+x}=m_\lambda(v,w)L_{v+w}\delta_x.$ Hence $L_vL_w=m_\lambda(v,w)L_{v+w}$ on the dense basis span and then everywhere. Also $L_0=I$ and $L_v^*=L_{-v}$, so $\delta_v\mapsto L_v$ extends linearly to a unital $*$-representation of the twisted finite-support algebra.
By [F1], this unital $*$-representation is contractive for the universal seminorm and extends to a representation $\Pi$ of $C^*_{\mathrm W}(V,\omega,\lambda)$ with $\Pi(\delta_v)=L_v$.

Fix a finite-dimensional real symplectic vector space $(V,\omega)$ and a real
parameter $\lambda$. A **Weyl system with parameter $\lambda$** on a nonzero
complex Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ is a map $W:V\to U(\mathcal H)$ such that
$$W(0)=I,\qquad W(v)W(w)=e^{-i\lambda\omega(v,w)/2}W(v+w)\quad(v,w\in V).$$
It is **regular** when, for every $v\in V$, the map
$t\mapsto W(tv)$ is strongly continuous on $\mathbb R$. It is
**irreducible** when the only closed subspaces invariant under every $W(v)$ are
$\{0\}$ and $\mathcal H$, as in
[[def-strongly-continuous-unitary-representation]].

Each $W(v)$ is unitary. Substituting $w=-v$ in the relation gives
$W(v)W(-v)=I$, because $\omega(v,-v)=0$; hence
$W(v)^*=W(-v)$. The scalar $\lambda$ is the central character parameter:
the associated representation of [[def-heisenberg-group-of-a-symplectic-vector-space]]
acts on $(0,t)$ by $e^{i\lambda t}I$.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

The metric space $\mathbb C$ is complete. A sequence $z_n=x_n+iy_n$ converges to $x+iy$ exactly when $x_n\to x$ and $y_n\to y$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]], [[thm-componentwise-convergence-and-completeness]].

$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $X$ be an LCH space with a fixed Radon measure $\mu$, and write
$C_c(X;\mathbb C)$ for the space of continuous complex-valued functions of
compact support ([[def-compact-support-c-c-and-c-zero-on-an-lch-space]]). A
complex-valued function on $X$ is **measurable** when its real and imaginary
parts are measurable, and it is **integrable** when its modulus is integrable
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). For
$p\in\{1,2\}$ the space $L^p(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ consists of the almost-everywhere
equivalence classes of measurable complex functions $f$ with
$$\|f\|_p:=\Bigl(\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu\Bigr)^{1/p}<\infty ,$$
the quotient and class notation being those of
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. The **modulus** $|f|$ of a
complex measurable function is measurable and depends only on the class of $f$
up to a null set, so $\|\cdot\|_p$ is well defined on classes; on classes it is
the norm of a complex normed space, and
$L^1(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ and $L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ are the complex Lebesgue
spaces used on this page.

([[def-left-haar-integral-and-left-haar-measure]]). Then
$C_c(G):=C_c(G;\mathbb C)$ and
$$L^p(G):=L^p(G,\mu;\mathbb C)\qquad(p\in\{1,2\}),$$
suppressing the measure from the notation; the Haar measure is kept fixed

$\|f\|_1$ and $\|f\|_2$ for the two norms.

$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero

norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. form $\omega((q,p),(q',p'))=q\cdot p'-p\cdot q'$ on $\mathbb R^{2n}$. On
$L^2(\mathbb R^n)$ define

$$\big(S_\lambda(q,p,t)f\big)(x) =e^{i\lambda t+i\lambda p\cdot(x-q/2)}f(x-q).$$
Then $S_\lambda$ is a strongly continuous unitary representation of [[def-heisenberg-group-of-a-symplectic-vector-space]], has central character $t\mapsto e^{i\lambda t}$, and its Weyl operators form an irreducible regular Weyl system with phase $e^{-i\lambda\omega/2}$.

Let $H=L^2(\mathbb R)$, let $\Omega\in H$ have norm one, and let
$H_n=L^2(\mathbb R^n)$ for $n\ge0$, where $H_0=\mathbb C$. For $m\ge n$
define $J_{n,m}:H_n\to H_m$ by

$$\big(J_{n,m}f\big)(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\prod_{j=n+1}^m\Omega(x_j).$$
The incomplete tensor product with reference vector $\Omega$ is the Hilbert completion of the compatible union of the $H_n$ under these maps. The vector $\Omega^{\infty}$ is the image of $1\in H_0$; more generally, the image of $f\in H_n$ has all coordinates after $n$ fixed at $\Omega$. For any unit vector $\Phi\in H$ and coordinate $j\ge1$, the **local rank-one projection** $P_j^\Phi$ applies $f\mapsto\langle f,\Phi\rangle\Phi$ in coordinate $j$ and the identity in the other coordinates. The proof verifies that the embeddings are well-defined and isometric and that $P_j^\Phi$ extends to an orthogonal projection on the completion.

Assume Countable Choice. In the one-mode Schrödinger Weyl system
$W(q,p)f(x)=e^{i(p x-pq/2)}f(x-q)$ on $L^2(\mathbb R)$, for $a>0$ put
$\Omega_a(x)=(a/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-ax^2/2}$. The weak Weyl average

$$A_a:=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{-aq^2/4-p^2/(4a)}W(q,p)\,dq\,dp$$
is the orthogonal projection $f\mapsto\langle f,\Omega_a\rangle\Omega_a$, and $\operatorname{span}\{W(q,p)\Omega_a:q,p\in\mathbb R\}$ is dense in $L^2(\mathbb R)$. If a bounded operator intertwines two regular one-mode Weyl systems with this phase, their averages exist and it intertwines them. In an incomplete tensor product of copies of this representation, $A_a$ acts on one coordinate as the rank-one projection onto $\Omega_a$ tensored with the identity on all other coordinates.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$. Finite linear combinations of indicator functions of
boxes are dense in $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
